title: Profiling kernel backpressure and quantization noise in multi-tenant workloads
body:
(continued)

Key observations:
1) Kernel backpressure correlates with quality regressions at the p99+ range. During bursts (Mix B) we see p99 latency increase by 3-6x for short requests when AWQ/int8 kernels are present. Those same p99 requests exhibit a median perplexity increase of 8-14% relative to fp32 baseline.

2) Kernel-switch-rate spikes precede quality drop windows. We measured a kernel-switch-rate jump from ~2 switches/sec to ~18 switches/sec during burst windows on affected GPUs. Each switch correlates with a small KV-cache eviction event (miss spikes from 4% to 18%), suggesting KV cache thrash as a mediating factor.

3) Per-kernel occupancy shows that low-precision kernels (int8-awq) have higher dispatch throughput but tighter occupancy margins. In mixed loads, they saturate compute lanes and force preemptive scheduling for dense-fp32 tasks, causing repeated short-lived kernel launches for the higher-precision codepath — amplifying context-switch overhead and increasing decode jitter.

4) FP8 shows smaller quality regressions but worse tail latency under microburst compared to AWQ. GPTQ behaved more stably in long-form paths but exhibited idiosyncratic token-level spikes when the scheduler attempted to pack heterogeneous shapes.

5) Noise amplification effect: isolated low-precision runs (single-tenant) show expected quality deltas (2-6% perplexity increase), but multi-tenant co-located runs amplify the apparent quality regression up to 3x. Hypothesis: interaction between kernel switches and KV cache thrash transiently changes token contexts (cache misses cause recompute or slower KV load), which interacts with low-precision rounding to increase token-by-token drift.

Representative numbers (13B model):
- Single-tenant AWQ: p95 latency 72ms, p99 180ms, perplexity +4.8% vs fp32.
- Multi-tenant AWQ mixed: p95 latency 85ms, p99 640ms, perplexity +13.2% vs fp32.
- Single-tenant GPTQ: p95 78ms, p99 210ms, perplexity +3.1%.
- Multi-tenant GPTQ mixed: p95 82ms, p99 320ms, perplexity +6.8%.

Qualitative failure modes observed:
- Short chat sequences where the second reply degrades (repeating tokens/ragged punctuation) after a high-concurrency spike. Manual diff shows slight token logits shift that compounds after ~8 tokens of generation.
- Long-form generation that loses coherence after a sudden scheduler preemption — often when switching back to a fp32 kernel mid-trajectory.

Root-cause hypothesis (draft):
- Primary driver is scheduler-induced microburst kernel mixing creating transient KV cache thrash and increasing context load time.
- Low-precision implementations are more sensitive to these micro-perturbations because rounding/noise accumulates faster when KV loads or compute reorderings occur.
- The combination (backpressure + low-precision kernel mixing) leads to amplified observed quality regressions independent of steady-state numeric fidelity.

Immediate mitigations tested (summary):
1) Kernel switchover cooldown: enforce 250ms cooldown between automatic kernel switches per-request. Result: kernel-switch-rate reduced by ~78% during bursts, p99 latency fell by ~45% in mixed runs, perplexity regressions dropped by ~6 percentage points.
2) KV-cache reservation: temporarily increase per-tenant cache slice size during bursts (auto-scale up to +2x) reduced KV miss spikes by half; coupled with cooldown gives best combined effect.
3) Preemptive traffic shaping: limit short-chat burst QPS via token-bucket at edge — reduces bursts but is user-visible.

Longer-term recommendations:
- Route-sensitive kernel allocation: prefer isolating low-precision inference to dedicated slices for high-churn tenants (profiling signal: switch-rate > 4/s). Implement scheduling hint to pin AWQ/GPTQ kernels to separate streams where capacity allows.
- Kernel mixing telemetry: add a per-request trace flag that logs kernel flavor transitions into the trace payload (for offline correlation with quality regressions).
- Context-consistent fallbacks: ensure when a kernel switchover happens mid-generation, the runtime either (a) completes the existing KV-context in the same kernel flavor or (b) performs a KV rewarm with fidelity-aware priority.
- Quant-quality SLOs: add a quality-regression guardrail that temporarily forces fp32 (or higher-fidelity profile) when p99-quality delta exceeds threshold over a sliding window.

Action items:
- Diego: file SERV-1248 follow-up to implement kernel switchover cooldown in experimental branch (target: v0.69).
- Priya: add kernel-transition traces and KV-cache event counters to the telemetry payload (task: TELE-886).
- Lena: run extended multi-tenant runs with fp8-packed-kernel-alpha pinned to dedicated slices to validate isolation hypothesis (due: 2026-02-10).
- Marcus: evaluate cost impact (tokens/$) for recommendations and produce a short runbook for Dedicated customers on isolation knobs (due: 2026-02-18).

Open questions / next experiments:
- Is the amplification effect consistent across different GPUs (H100 vs A100) and with MIG enabled? Need a cross-arch sweep.
- Does increasing kernel launch batching window (hold small requests for 10ms to batch) help or harm tail quality? Batching reduces switches but increases latency for short queries. Tradeoffs to quantify.
- Is there a practical per-tenant heuristic that balances cost and quality without manual isolation? Explore machine-learned routing policy.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an initial field study – numbers are noisy across runs. We believe the qualitative effect is strong and actionable (cooldown + cache reservation combination worked best).
- Please point to any missing telemetry that would make causality stronger (I suspect we need per-kernel per-request KV-lookup timing).
